body:
International Morse code is built on a single measure of time: the unit. ITU-R Recommendation M.1677-1 describes every signal and every silence as a whole number of units. A dot lasts 1 unit. A dash lasts 3 units.

The silences are timed too. The space between elements of the same character lasts 1 unit. The space between two characters lasts 3 units. The space between two words lasts 7 units. Read together, the pattern is easy to remember: a one-unit gap keeps elements together, a dash-length gap separates characters, and a seven-unit gap marks a new word.

To practice, choose any comfortable unit length and count in whole units. A character made of one dot followed by one dash takes 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 units from start to finish, and then 3 silent units pass before the next character begins. At the end of a word, that silence stretches to 7 units instead. Tapping a steady beat and counting helps keep each duration in proportion.

The ITU source states that maintaining these exact timing ratios ensures legibility across noisy radio channels. Because the gaps separate elements, characters and words, keeping them proportional is what lets a listener hear where each boundary falls. This entry covers timing only; it does not list character codes or recommend a sending speed.

summary: Time International Morse code in whole units: a dot is 1 unit and a dash is 3. Gaps are 1 unit within a character, 3 units between characters and 7 units between words.
title: Count the silences in Morse code
